title: Commodious sense: venial by event (pardoned) vs mortal by event (actually damning)
source_text: XXV. Et primo quidem patiuntur venialia dici peccata quae actu veniam consequuntur, propter peccatoris fidem & resipiscentiam, utut in se gravissima sint: singulari vero quadam ratione mortalia, quae mortem & perditionem aeternam peccantibus reipsa afferunt, propter ipsorum incredulitatem & impoenitentiam. Quod Schola Romana vocat mortale & veniale ex eventu, ut antea observatum fuit.
pass_a_gloss: And first indeed they allow sins to be called venial which in act obtain pardon because of the sinner’s faith and repentance, however most grievous they are in themselves: but by a certain singular reason mortal those which in very deed bring eternal death and perdition upon sinners because of their unbelief and impenitence. Which the Roman School calls mortal and venial from the event, as was observed before.
pass_b_english: First commodious use: ‘venial’ for sins actually pardoned through faith and repentance—even if huge in themselves.
‘Mortal’ then marks sins that in fact damn through unbelief and impenitence—Rome’s ‘from the event.’

choices.why: Concessive: gravity in themselves does not bar the label.
